According to tradition, she was a young virgin who was a member of the Christian community in Antioch, Syria. She was arrested and taken to the Roman governor, who tried to force her to deny her faith and offer sacrifices to the Roman gods. Marieta refused, and was subjected to various forms of torture, including being exposed to wild animals. She miraculously survived these ordeals, and was eventually beheaded. Her relics were later enshrined in a church in Antioch, and she is now venerated as a saint in both the Eastern and Western Churches.

Marieta of Cologne, also known as Saint Maria Magdalena, was a 13th century German nun who is said to have lived in the monastery of St. Ursula in Cologne. She was renowned for her piety and her visions, which she claimed to have received from God. One of her most famous visions was of the suffering souls in purgatory, who begged her to pray for them and offer Masses for their release. Marieta became known as the 'Comforter of the Suffering', and her intercession was believed to bring great consolation to those in need of spiritual comfort. She died in 1253, and was canonized in 1604.
